God requires obedience to his covenant (verses 1–10)

God has never promised to bless rational creatures while they deliberately continue in disobedience.

Pardon and acceptance are freely promised to everyone who believes.

But no one can be saved while refusing God's command to repent, believe in Christ, separate from sin and the world, deny self and walk in newness of life.

People readily listen when speakers describe doctrines, promises and privileges.

Yet when the subject turns to duty, they often refuse to hear.

Idolatry cannot protect a nation from judgment (verses 11–17)

Evil pursues sinners and entangles them in traps from which they cannot free themselves.

In their distress, their many gods and altars provided no help.

People whose own prayers will not be accepted cannot presume to benefit from someone else's prayers.

A mere profession of religion does no good.

When trouble came, the people had relied on that profession, but God rejected it.

His altar could give them no comfort.

Remembering God's earlier favors toward them would not console them amid judgment.

Nor could those favors be used as a reason why he must rescue them now.

Every sin committed against the Lord is also a sin against ourselves.

Sooner or later its consequences will prove that true.

Jeremiah is threatened by people from his own town (verses 18–23)

Jeremiah's book reveals much about his personal suffering.

He lived in deeply troubled times.

Men from his own town secretly planned his death.

They hoped to shorten his life.

But Jeremiah outlived most of his enemies.

They also wanted to destroy his reputation.

Yet his memory has survived until today, and it will continue to be honored as long as time endures.

God knows every secret plan of those who oppose his servants and his people.

When he chooses, he can disclose those plans.

God's justice is a source of terror to wicked people but a comfort to those who trust him.

When others wrong us, we have a God to whom we can entrust our cause.

We should commit the matter to him.

And we must watch our own attitudes, lest evil overcome us.

Through patient prayer for our enemies and kindness toward them, we can overcome evil with good.

The disobedient Jews reproved. ( [Jer.11.1-Jer.11.10] Jr 11:1-10) Their utter ruin. ( [Jer.11.11-Jer.11.17] Jr 11:11-17) The people would be destroyed who sought the prophet's life. ( [Jer.11.18-Jer.11.23] Jr 11:18-23)
Verses 1-10 God never promised to bestow blessings on his rational creatures, while they persist in wilful disobedience. Pardon and acceptance are promised freely to all believers; but no man can be saved who does not obey the command of God to repent, to believe in Christ, to separate from sin and the world, to choose self-denial and newness of life. In general, men will hearken to those who speak of doctrines, promises, and privileges; but when duties are mentioned, they will not bend their ear.
[Jer.11.11-Jer.11.17]
Verses 11-17 Evil pursues sinners, and entangles them in snares, out of which they cannot free themselves. Now, in their distress, their many gods and many altars stand them in no stead. And those whose own prayers will not be heard, cannot expect benefit from the prayers of others. Their profession of religion shall prove of no use. When trouble came upon them, they made this their confidence, but God has rejected it. His altar shall yield them no satisfaction. The remembrance of God's former favours to them shall be no comfort under troubles; and his remembrance of them shall be no argument for their relief. Every sin against the Lord is a sin against ourselves, and so it will be found sooner or later.
[Jer.11.18-Jer.11.23]
Verses 18-23 The prophet Jeremiah tells much concerning himself, the times he lived in being very troublesome. Those of his own city plotted how they might cause his death. They thought to end his days, but he outlived most of his enemies; they thought to blast his memory, but it lives to this day, and will be blessed while time lasts. God knows all the secret designs of his and his people's enemies, and can, when he pleases, make them known. God's justice is a terror to the wicked, but a comfort to the godly. When we are wronged, we have a God to commit our cause to, and it is our duty to commit it to him. We should also look well to our own spirits, that we are not overcome with evil, but that by patient continuance in praying for our enemies, and in kindness to them, we may overcome evil with good.

Why do the wicked prosper? (verses 1–6)

When God's ways are darkest to us, we must continue to think rightly of his character.

He has never acted unjustly toward any creature.

When we cannot understand a particular event affecting ourselves or others, we must return to the general truths we know.

The Lord is righteous.

God knows the condition of every heart.

He sees the deceit of the hypocrite and the sincerity of the upright.

Judgment will eventually pull wicked people out of their prosperous pasture like sheep led to slaughter.

The land became barren because of the sins of those living in it.

The Lord also corrected Jeremiah himself.

The opposition he had encountered at Anathoth was small compared with what awaited him from Judah's rulers.

Our grief over evil in the world is often mixed with irritability about the trouble that evil causes us.

We live in favored times and face comparatively small difficulties.

How would we behave if called to endure what faithful believers in former generations suffered?

The Lord gives his beloved people over to judgment (verses 7–13)

God's people had been beloved by him, precious in his sight.

Yet their conduct led him to hand them over to their enemies.

Many professing churches become like speckled birds.

Their lives mix true religious profession with the world's fashions, pursuits and corruptions.

God's people may be a spectacle to others.

But in this case they had made themselves one through their own foolishness, leaving themselves vulnerable to the creatures called to prey upon them.

The whole land would become desolate.

Until judgment actually fell, almost no one would give God's warning serious attention.

When he raises his hand and people refuse to see, they may be made to feel.

Neither silver nor gold helps in the day of divine anger.

Attempts to escape suffering without repentance and deeds appropriate to it will end in confusion.

Even neighboring nations may receive mercy (verses 14–17)

The Lord would defend the cause of his people against their wicked neighbors.

But afterward he would show mercy even to those nations, if they learned the true faith.

Henry sees this as possibly looking ahead to the day when the fullness of the Gentiles comes in.

Anyone who wants a share in God's people's inheritance and hopes to reach the same final happiness must learn their ways and walk in them.

The ruined linen belt (verses 1–11)

The prophets often taught through visible signs, and here God explains the sign himself (Jeremiah 13:9–11).

Israel had been like the belt that clung closely to its owner.

God had caused the people to cling to him through the law he gave them, the prophets he sent and the blessings he bestowed.

But through idolatry and sin, they had buried themselves in foreign soil and become entangled with other nations.

They were now so corrupted that, like the ruined belt, they were no longer useful.

If we are proud of learning, power or outward privileges, God is just in allowing them to wither.

Our minds need to awaken to guilt and danger.

Yet no warning will truly change us without the Holy Spirit's influence.

The jars of judgment and a call to repent (verses 12–17)

Just as jars are made to hold wine, so the people's sins had made them vessels prepared for divine wrath.

They would be filled with judgments until those judgments led them to destroy one another.

Jeremiah begged them to give glory to God by confessing sin, humbling themselves in repentance and returning to his service.

If they refused, they would be carried into foreign lands, still enveloped in the darkness of idolatry and wickedness.

Anyone with a compassionate heart is moved by suffering, whether witnessed or only anticipated.

But a godly heart should grieve especially over the afflictions of the Lord's flock.

No one can cleanse a sinful nature without God (verses 18–27)

The message was addressed to King Jehoiakim and his queen.

Their suffering would be great.

Why had it come upon them?

Because they had persisted stubbornly in sin.

People cannot change the natural color of their skin by their own efforts.

Henry uses that biblical image to express how morally impossible it is for unrenewed sinners to reform themselves by their own strength.

Sin is the soul's corruption and disfigurement.

We were formed in it and cannot free ourselves through our own power.

But Almighty grace can accomplish what no human being can.

Neither inherited corruption nor long-established habits of sin can prevent God's Spirit, who creates new life, from transforming a person.

The Lord asks Jerusalem whether she is determined to refuse cleansing.

If someone enslaved by sin feels that changing deeply rooted desires is as impossible as changing human nature, that person should not despair.

What is impossible for human beings is possible with God.

Let us seek help from the One mighty to save.

Drought and prayerful confession (verses 1–9)

The people wept, but theirs was more a cry over distress and sin than the cry of genuine prayer.

Let us be thankful for water before its absence teaches us how precious it is.

Farmers depend completely on God's Providence: unless he waters their furrows, they cannot plow and sow with confidence.

Even wild animals suffered pitiably under the drought.

The people were slow to pray, but Jeremiah prayed for them and humbly confessed their sin.

Our sins both accuse us and testify against us.

The strongest arguments in our prayers are those drawn from the glory of God's own name.

We should dread his departure more than the loss of any created comfort.

God had given Israel his word on which to hope.

In prayer, his glory should concern us more than our immediate relief.

If we return to the Lord, he will save us to the glory of his grace.

False prophets and their hearers face judgment (verses 10–16)

The Lord called the Jews “this people” rather than “my people.” They had abandoned his service; he would judge them according to their sins.

God forbade Jeremiah to intercede for them.

The false prophets were most guilty, and the Lord pronounced judgment upon them.

But the people themselves wanted to hear their false assurances, so they too would face judgment.

False teachers lead people to expect peace and salvation without repentance, faith, conversion or holiness of life.

Anyone who willingly believes a lie cannot offer deception as an excuse.

People who reject the warning will experience the very judgment they were told not to fear.

The prophet pleads for the covenant and mercy (verses 17–22)

Jeremiah confessed his own sins and the people's sins, appealing to the Lord's covenant.

No Gentile idol could help them.

Even the heavens could not give rain by themselves without their Creator.

God will always preserve people who plead before his mercy seat.

He will heal every genuinely repentant sinner.

Even when God does not grant the national relief for which we pray, he will certainly bless with salvation everyone who confesses sin and seeks his mercy.

Verses 1-9 The people were in tears. But it was rather the cry of their trouble, and of their sin, than of their prayer. Let us be thankful for the mercy of water, that we may not be taught to value it by feeling the want of it. See what dependence husbandmen have upon the Divine providence. They cannot plough nor sow in hope, unless God water their furrows. The case even of the wild beasts was very pitiable. The people are not forward to pray, but the prophet prays for them. We should dread God's departure, more than the removal of our creature-comforts. He has given Israel his word to hope in. False teachers encourage men to expect peace and salvation, without repentance, faith, conversion, and holiness of life. But those who believe a lie must not plead if for an excuse. They shall feel what they say they will not fear.

Verses 17-22 Jeremiah acknowledged his own sins, and those of the people, but pleaded with the Lord to remember his covenant. He will heal every truly repenting sinner. Even if Moses and Samuel stood before God to plead for the people, they would not prevail.

Henry emphasizes that this is a hypothetical example, not a statement that the prophets actually stand praying in heaven.

He argues on that basis against the belief that saints in heaven pray for those on earth.

The Jews would suffer different kinds of misery under the Lord's righteous judgment.

Survivors would be driven into captivity like chaff scattered from grain.

The city once filled with people would become desolate.

Bad examples and the misuse of authority can have deadly consequences even after people die or repent of their crimes.

We should fear causing another person to fall into sin.

The prophet is despised, but God's plan stands (verses 10–14)

Jeremiah received reproach when people should have blessed him and thanked God for giving them his ministry.

Whatever difficulties God's people face, they may find sufficient strength in knowing their latter end will be good.

The Lord then confronted the nation.

Could all its strength resist his decree or stop the army of the Chaldeans?

The enemy would treat Jeremiah kindly while those with large estates would suffer severely.

Every part of the country had contributed to national guilt, and each must take its share of shame.

The Lord calls Jeremiah away from distrust (verses 15–21)

It is comforting to have a God whose knowledge embraces everything.

Jeremiah appealed to him for protection against his enemies, persecutors and slanderers.

When a minister is despised, a clear conscience can still provide encouragement.

Yet Jeremiah complained that he had gained little pleasure from his service.

Even good people can lose much of religion's joy when they indulge a fretful and restless natural disposition.

God called the prophet to abandon distrust and return to his task.

If he remained faithful, the Lord would deliver him from his enemies.

Those who stay close to God and serve him sincerely will be rescued from trouble or carried safely through it.

Many events appear frightening though they can do no final harm to a true believer in Christ.

The destruction of the wicked described. ( [Jer.15.1-Jer.15.9] Jr 15:1-9) The prophet laments such messages, and is reproved. ( [Jer.15.10-Jer.15.14] Jr 15:10-14) He supplicates pardon, and is promised protection. ( [Jer.15.15-Jer.15.21] Jr 15:15-21)

[Jer.15.15-Jer.15.21]

The Lord called the prophet to cease from his distrust, and to return to his work. If he attended thereto, he might be assured the Lord would deliver him from his enemies. Those who are with God, and faithful to him, he will deliver from trouble or carry through it. Many things appear frightful, which do not at all hurt a real believer in Christ.

Jeremiah lives in expectation of the nation's ruin (verses 1–9)

The prophet was to behave as a person expecting the destruction of his country very soon.

Because distressing days lay ahead, God told him to refrain from marriage, customary mourning for the dead and celebration.

Those wanting others to believe God's word must show through personal self-denial that they believe it themselves.

All peace—inward and outward, within the family and among the public—comes from the Lord's kindness and mercy.

When he removes peace, distress follows.

In certain extraordinary circumstances it may be right to abstain from acts that are normally our duty.

We should never cling tightly to the pleasures and concerns of this passing life.

The judgment is just (verses 10–13)

The people's response seems to have been a complaint against God.

Rather than humbling themselves and admitting sin, they justified themselves, as though the Lord had treated them unjustly.

But God answered plainly.

They were more stubborn than their ancestors.

Each one walked according to the plans of his or her own heart.

Since they refused to listen, they would be taken to an unfamiliar country.

If they had enjoyed God's favor, even the land of captivity could have been pleasant.

Restoration will foreshadow salvation through Christ (verses 14–21)

The rescue from Babylon would be remembered instead of the original exodus from Egypt.

It would also picture spiritual redemption and what Henry describes as a later deliverance of the church from antichristian oppression.

No sin can be hidden from God or overlooked by him.

He can send instruments of judgment like fishermen who use deception or hunters who pursue with force.

But Jeremiah, rejoicing in the promised mercy, addressed the Lord as his strength and refuge.

The return from captivity would be a picture of the far greater salvation accomplished by the Messiah.

The nations had often seen God's power in his anger.

They would also recognize him as the strength of his people and their refuge in times of trouble.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe fatal consequences of the idolatry of the Jews.1–4The happiness of the man that trusts in God; the end of the opposite character.5–11The malice of the prophet's enemies.12–18The observance of the sabbath.19–27
Sin written on the heart (verses 1–4)

People often scarcely notice the sins they commit.

Yet every sin is recorded before God, and all are so engraved upon the human heart that conscience will eventually recall them.

What is engraved in the heart becomes visible in a person's conduct.

Our actions reveal the desires and purposes within us.

How much reason we have to humble ourselves before the Lord when we consider our sinfulness in his sight!

Let us depend upon his mercy and grace.

Ask him to search and test our hearts, keep us from being deceived by them and create in us, through his Spirit, a new, clean and holy nature.

The desert shrub and the fruitful tree (verses 5–11)

Someone who trusts in human beings is like a lonely shrub in a desert—the poor and useless product of barren land.

People who depend on their own righteousness and strength, imagining they can do without Christ, have made human flesh their support.

They cannot prosper in spiritual grace or comfort.

But those who make God their hope flourish like an evergreen tree.

They remain settled in peace and contentment, with no need for panic in a year of drought.

God supplies every comfort they truly need, even when created comforts are absent.

They do not stop bearing the fruit of holiness and good works.

The heart and conscience of fallen humanity are more deceitful than anything else.

They call evil good and good evil.

They pronounce peace upon people who have no true peace.

This is how desperate its corruption is.

Conscience should correct the errors of our other faculties.

But when conscience itself becomes the leader in self-deception, our situation is especially serious.

We cannot fully know our hearts or how they will behave in a sudden temptation.

Who can understand their own errors?

Still less can we fully know or safely depend on other people's hearts.

Anyone accepting God's testimony about this will learn to watch the heart and will recognize many useful lessons for conduct.

Much about our own motives and those of others will remain unknown to us.

But nothing within us is hidden from God.

People may be deceived.

He cannot be deceived.

Those who acquire wealth dishonestly will not truly enjoy it.

At death the worldly person must leave possessions behind.

The wealth cannot follow into eternity, but its guilt can.

Someone may spend a whole life acquiring wealth, brood over it anxiously and never receive satisfaction.

Sinful gain may disappear altogether.

Let us become wise in time: earn honestly and give generously, so that we may be prepared for eternity.

The Lord is a fountain of comfort (verses 12–18)

Jeremiah acknowledged God's goodness in establishing true worship.

The Lord is an overflowing fountain of comfort, forever fresh and clear like springwater.

The sinful world's pleasures resemble muddy puddles.

The prophet asked for the Lord's healing and saving mercy.

He appealed to God as the One who knew how faithfully he had fulfilled his prophetic calling.

He humbly asked the Lord to acknowledge and defend him in the service to which he had called him.

Whatever wounds or diseases afflict our hearts and consciences, let us seek healing from God.

His hands can bind up troubled consciences and heal broken hearts.

He can cure the deepest corruption of our nature, giving us reason to praise his name.

Keep the Sabbath holy (verses 19–27)

Jeremiah had to set before both rulers and ordinary people the command to keep the Sabbath day holy.

They were to obey the fourth commandment.

God promised renewed prosperity if they obeyed.

The Sabbath is appointed for rest, not ordinary labor, except when necessity requires work.

We should watch carefully against treating the day as common.

Even our souls should not be weighed down with worldly business and anxieties on the Sabbath.

Henry compares religious life to a river: the stream runs deep or shallow according to whether the banks of Sabbath observance are maintained or neglected.

The care with which a people observe this ordinance, or the indifference they show toward it, reveals much about their spiritual condition.

Everyone should work through personal example and attention to family life to prevent its neglect.

National good matters, but even more important is the salvation of souls.

The potter, the clay and God's righteous rule (verses 1–10)

As Jeremiah watched the potter at work, God impressed two great truths upon his mind.

First, the Lord possesses the authority and power to shape and dispose of kingdoms and nations as he chooses.

He may deal with us according to his wisdom.

For clay to argue with the potter would be absurd—and so is our disputing against God's right to rule.

Second, God always acts according to settled principles of goodness and justice.

When judgment is approaching, we may be sure that sin has brought it upon us.

But sincere conversion and turning away from sin can prevent the threatened judgment—whether for individuals, families or nations.

Sinful liberty is the worst slavery (verses 11–17)

Sinners call unrestrained living freedom.

Yet slavery to sinful desires is the most dreadful form of slavery.

Judah had abandoned God for idols.

A thirsty person who reaches a cool and refreshing stream would not ordinarily abandon that reliable water for an uncertain supply elsewhere.

But Israel abandoned the ancient paths established by God's law.

Instead of walking along the safe highway, the people chose a path where they were bound to stumble.

Such is the way of idolatry and wrongdoing.

It left them miserable and their land desolate.

Earthly troubles can be endured if God continues to favor us through them.

But if he is displeased and refuses his help, we are undone.

Multitudes turn from the Lord and his Christ and leave the ancient paths to follow religious ways invented by themselves.

What will they do on the day of judgment?

Jeremiah's enemies plot against him (verses 18–23)

When Jeremiah called the people to repent, they plotted against him instead of obeying.

Sinners treat the great Intercessor in a similar way.

They speak against Christ and in that sense crucify him afresh, even while his blood pleads on their behalf in heaven.

But the prophet had performed the duty God gave him toward the people.

That consciousness of duty would be a source of rejoicing in a time of trouble.

By the type of breaking an earthen vessel, Jeremiah is to predict the destruction of Judah.

The coming ruin of Jerusalem (verses 1–9)

Jeremiah had to announce the destruction approaching Judah and Jerusalem.

Rulers and ordinary people alike needed to hear this message.

Jerusalem's holiness had once made it the joy of the whole earth.

But sin had made the city a place of shame and disgrace before the whole earth.

There is only one way to escape God's justice:

Flee to his mercy.

The shattered earthen vessel (verses 10–15)

Once a potter's earthen vessel has hardened and been broken into pieces, no one can fit it together again as before.

So Judah and Jerusalem would be shattered by the Chaldeans, just as Jeremiah broke the vessel.

No human hand could repair the destruction.

Yet if the people returned to the Lord, he could heal them.

The people had filled Topheth with people slaughtered in sacrifices to idols.

Therefore the Lord would fill the city with those killed as a judgment upon their sin.

Whatever human beings imagine, God will prove as terrible toward unrepentant wrongdoing as Scripture has said.

Unbelief cannot make either his promises or his warnings ineffective.

Sinners are responsible for their own stubbornness.

If they refuse to hear God's word, it is because they have deliberately closed their ears.

We must pray that God's grace will rescue us from hardness of heart and contempt for his word and commandments.

Pashhur becomes an object of terror (verses 1–6)

Pashhur struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks.

The prophet remained silent until God gave him a message.

To confirm that message, Pashhur received the name “Terror on every side.”

It describes a person not simply suffering but despairing, not merely surrounded by danger but terrified on every side.

Wicked people may experience dreadful fear even where no genuine danger appears.

God can make even the boldest sinner a terror to himself.

People who refuse to hear God's prophets expose their faults may later be forced to hear those same accusations from their own consciences.

How miserable is someone whose conscience has made that person a constant terror!

Friends may abandon such a person.

God may leave a sinner alive in deep misery as a visible reminder of his justice.

The Lord strengthens Jeremiah to keep serving (verses 7–13)

Jeremiah complained about the insults and injuries he endured.

But Henry notes a possible reading of verse 7:

“You persuaded me, and I was persuaded; you were stronger than I and overcame me by the influence of your Spirit.”

When we know that we are following the path of duty God has given us, we act weakly and foolishly if discouragement makes us wish we had never begun the work.

Jeremiah discovered that divine grace was powerful enough to keep him serving despite the temptation to abandon his calling.

Whatever wrongs others do to us, we must entrust judgment to the God who says, “I will repay.”

The prophet became deeply conscious of God's presence, his protection and the promises upon which he relied.

He therefore urged himself and others to glorify the Lord.

When God's people lay their concerns openly before him, he enables them to see his deliverance.

Jeremiah laments the day of his birth (verses 14–18)

When grace wins a victory over temptation, it is right to feel ashamed of our foolishness and to marvel at God's kindness.

We should also be warned to guard our minds more carefully when another trial comes.

See how powerful a temptation Jeremiah faced—and how God's help enabled him to overcome it!

In his bitterness, Jeremiah became angry that his first breath had not been his last.

These lamentations were recorded not to teach us to repeat the same wishes, but to give us needed warnings.

People who think they stand securely must take care lest they fall.

We should pray daily:

“Lead us not into temptation.”

How frail, inconsistent and sinful we are!

How foolish and unnatural our wishes become when discontent rules our hearts!

Consider Jesus Christ, who endured the opposition of sinners against himself, so that we will not become weary or fainthearted during our much smaller trials.

Whatever injuries are done to us, we must leave them to that God to whom vengeance belongs, and who has said, I will repay. While we remember that these wishes are not recorded for us to utter the like, we may learn good lessons from them. How foolish and unnatural are the thoughts and wishes of our hearts, when we yield to discontent!
